chunks: Test points on high-speed or sensitive signals. The question: Should you use test points on high-speed or sensitive signals? Why?
On the fastest and most sensitive signals, a test point is not free.
The pad adds a little capacitance (stored charge that blunts sharp changes) and a stub, and these disturb the signal you want to measure.
So for these signals you use a special kind of point, such as an in-line pad or a coaxial connector, or you use a built-in self-test instead of a pad.
Picture a fast channel of water with a small side basin cut into its bank. A smooth, slow flow barely notices the basin.
A sharp, rushing wave slaps into it, and part of the wave bounces back up the channel. A stub on a fast net is that basin. The faster the edge, the more the pad matters.
One caveat: a long stub also rings like a struck bell at certain frequencies (it resonates), which adds extra harm.
The line (50 ohms source, line, 50 ohms termination) with a test pad tapped on. Without R iso the 1 picofarads pad hangs straight on the line and reflects about 24.
5% at 100 picoseconds. With a 500 ohms resistor at the tap, the initial reflection is about minus 4. 8%, decaying with τ about (R iso + Z0/2)·C about 0.
5 nanoseconds, but the pad now sees a low-pass.
Edge: the fast rise or fall of a signal; its rise time is how quickly it changes. Stub: a short dead-end spur of copper joining the pad to the signal.
Reflection: part of the edge bouncing back from a bump in the line. In-line pad: a pad that the trace itself runs through, so there is no stub.
Built-in self-test (BIST): the chip checking its own link, so no probe is needed.
A pad with its stub adds about 0. 5 picofarads to a typical 50 ohms signal line. With a 100 picoseconds edge, about 12. 5 % of the step reflects. At 1 picofarads it is about 24.
5 %. A 10 mm open stub also resonates near 3. 75 gigahertz, and a 100 picoseconds edge carries frequencies up to about 3. 5 gigahertz. So the pad would visibly distort the signal.
The fix is an in-line pad, a tiny stub, or measuring at the receiver. That is the whole idea.
"I avoid or special-case them on fast and sensitive nets.
A pad plus stub adds roughly half a picofarad that reflects about 12% on a 50 ohm line at 100 picoseconds edges, and the stub can resonate and close an eye.
On sensitive analog nodes, pads and probes add loading, leakage and pickup.
So I use in-line pads, tiny stubs with an isolation resistor, coax footprints, buffered monitors or built-in eye scan and measure at the receiver."
